segments.name: The House on the South Bank

stops.name: Via de' Bardi, born Mone di Geri di Ricco di Bardo
stops.date_confidence: No birth record survives. D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice offers no date and states the inference as an inference. c.1260 is worked backward from his being an adult party to property acts in 1280 and reportedly a widower by then; the month and day are unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: No book records the day. His birth year is worked backward from parchment: he is transacting land as a grown man in 1280, so he was born before, and no source will say more. He is Mone di Geri di Ricco di Bardo, a name stacked four deep so the notaries can tell him from the other Simoni of his house, and there are many of those. The Bardi hold the south bank. Towers, houses in a row along a road that already carries their name, the parish of Santa Lucia dei Magnoli, an oath-bound kindred large enough to put armed men in the street.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
Isidoro Del Lungo, Beatrice nella vita e nella poesia del secolo XIII (Milan: Hoepli, 1891)
suggested_refs: Via de' Bardi and the church of Santa Lucia dei Magnoli, Oltrarno, Florence
Palazzo Canigiani, Via de' Bardi, originally palazzo de' Bardi

stops.name: Via de' Bardi, the company and the name
stops.date_confidence: Undated and conventional; the year is an ordering device only. The Bardi company's Oltrarno seat and its 1345 collapse are well documented. Simone's personal role in the company is attested in no source consulted, and this stop marks that gap rather than an event. The research pool sited the company at the Mercato Vecchio; no source supports that, and the Oltrarno siting is used instead.
stops.campa: The Compagnia dei Bardi lends to kings. Its factors keep desks in London and Bruges and Naples, English wool money moves through its ledgers, and in 1345 its failure on royal debt will be the loudest bankruptcy in Christendom. Nearly every popular account of Simone borrows that greatness and calls him a banker. The company's surviving books do not name him, as partner or factor or holder of an account. What the records show him doing is buying land, standing surety for other men, and riding out when the commune calls.
sources: Maria Paola Zanoboni, 'Portinari, Beatrice', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 85 (Treccani, 2016)
Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: The Bardi company's ledgers and the 1345 failure on English royal debt
Via de' Bardi, Oltrarno, the family's documented seat

stops.name: Via de' Bardi, the death of Geri di Ricco
stops.date_confidence: Attested only negatively and by implication: the February 1281 conveyance styles Simone son of the late Geri di Ricco di Bardo, so Geri was dead by then. No death date, place, or cause is recorded. Dated 1281 with month and day defaulted. The underlying text is a seventeenth-century Strozzi transcription, not a medieval original.
stops.campa: By the time the notary writes him into a parchment, Simone is styled Mone, son of the late Geri di Ricco di Bardo de' Bardi. The father is dead, and that phrase is the whole of what survives of him in this line of the record. Simone and his brother Cecchino hold the patrimony together now, and for the next twenty-five years they will pass pieces of it back and forth between them, buying, leasing, selling, standing behind each other's obligations. Cecchino appears in nearly every property act his brother leaves behind.
sources: Domenico Savini and Samuele Masi, 'Messer Simone e madonna Bice: nuovi e inediti documenti su Beatrice Portinari', adhocnews.it, 17 July 2026
BNCF, Magliabechiana cl. XXV n. 591 (olim Carte Strozziane 1223), transcription by Carlo Strozzi, c.1635
suggested_refs: The lost parchment of 26 February 1281 and Carlo Strozzi's copy of it

segments.name: The Land at al Buco and the Consent of Bice

stops.name: Pieve di Ripoli, the land and house at al Buco
stops.date_confidence: Reported, not attested. The medieval original is lost; the evidence is Carlo Strozzi's transcription of about 1635 (BNCF, Magliabechiana cl. XXV n. 591), published only in Savini and Masi's non-peer-reviewed 2026 article. The coordinate is the pieve of San Pietro a Ripoli; al Buco itself cannot be located, the piviere having held sixteen suffragan churches in the late thirteenth century.
stops.campa: East of the city, where the Arno bends toward the hills, the pieve of San Pietro a Ripoli gathers sixteen parishes under it. In one of them, San Lorenzo, at a spot called al Buco, Simone and his brother buy land and a house from their cousin Bartolo. This is the ground the following winter's act will move again. The place-name is common, the piviere is wide, and the parchment that held the description burned or rotted or was carted off centuries ago. What is left is a copy an antiquary made in the 1630s. Which field was it? Nobody can now say.
sources: Domenico Savini and Samuele Masi, adhocnews.it, 17 July 2026, citing BNCF Magliabechiana cl. XXV n. 591
suggested_refs: The pieve di San Pietro a Ripoli, Bagno a Ripoli, and its sixteen suffragan parishes

stops.name: Florence, the death of Gemma dei Pulci
stops.date_confidence: Reported, not attested, and contested. The date comes from Savini and Masi's 2026 reading of a later dowry-restoration proceeding (ASFi, Notarile Antecosimiano, notary Bonaiuto di Nolfo, vol. 2950, pp. 90ff); the same article carries internally corrupt dates elsewhere and no scholarly edition corroborates it. It also stands in tension with Zanoboni's dating of the Portinari marriage to 1280 at the latest.
stops.campa: His first wife is Gemma dei Pulci. She bears him at least one child, a daughter called Bartola, whose dowry will still be in litigation years afterward, and that lawsuit is the only reason anyone knows Gemma existed. She dies in the autumn. A Florentine magnate does not stay unmarried long, and within months, on the argument of the men who found the document, he is negotiating for a girl of fifteen from the other bank of the river. The widower is perhaps twenty and perhaps thirty-five. The record does not say which.
sources: Domenico Savini and Samuele Masi, adhocnews.it, 17 July 2026, citing ASFi, Notarile Antecosimiano, notary Bonaiuto di Nolfo, vol. 2950
Maria Paola Zanoboni, 'Portinari, Beatrice', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani, 2016)
suggested_refs: The dowry-restoration proceeding of Bartola di Simone de' Bardi

stops.name: Portinari houses, the marriage to Bice di Folco
stops.date_confidence: The fact of the marriage is attested by Folco Portinari's will of 15 January 1288. The date is contested and is not resolved here: Zanoboni's Dizionario Biografico entry holds that the marriage 'sembra debba risalire al 1280 almeno', while Savini and Masi argue for a narrow January to February 1281 window after Gemma dei Pulci's reported death. 1280 is used to order the segment; month and day are unknown and defaulted. Pin inherited from dante.journey.json.
stops.campa: Folco di Ricovero Portinari is rich, a prior of the city, founder of the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova, and the father of daughters who must be placed. He places Bice with the Bardi. She is about fifteen; Simone is at least twice that, a widower and a knight. No marriage record survives: not the contract, not the dowry figure, not the day. What survives is her father's will, drawn eight years later, which leaves her fifty lire because her dowry is already paid and calls her the wife of dominus Simon de Bardis.
sources: Maria Paola Zanoboni, 'Portinari, Beatrice', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 85 (Treccani, 2016)
Folco Portinari's testament, 15 January 1288, printed by Isidoro Del Lungo (1891)
Domenico Savini and Samuele Masi, adhocnews.it, 17 July 2026
suggested_refs: The Portinari houses and the church of Santa Margherita de' Cerchi, Florence
The hospital of Santa Maria Nuova, founded by Folco Portinari 1285-86

stops.name: The Oltrarno, the bride crosses the river
stops.date_confidence: Inference, not record. No document names the house the couple occupied. The Bardi holdings on Via de' Bardi in Oltrarno, in particular the palace later called Canigiani, are the family's documented seat, and residence with the husband's kin is the ordinary pattern. Dated 1280 only to order the segment; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The Portinari live in the tight streets north of the Arno, by the small church of Santa Margherita de' Cerchi where the family keeps its chapel. The Bardi live across the water, on the road under the hill of San Giorgio. No deed names the room she was given. It is fifteen minutes on foot over the Ponte a Rubaconte, and it is the whole distance of her life: out of her father's household into her husband's, into a quarter of armed kinsmen and towers under the hill.
sources: Marco Santagata's reconstruction of Dante's Florence, as summarized in the consulted secondary literature
Maria Paola Zanoboni, 'Portinari, Beatrice', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani, 2016)
suggested_refs: The Ponte a Rubaconte, now Ponte alle Grazie, built 1237
Palazzo Canigiani, Via de' Bardi, originally palazzo de' Bardi

stops.name: Santa Lucia dei Magnoli, the consent of Bice
stops.date_confidence: Dated 26 February 1280 Florentine style, which is 26 February 1281 modern. Reported, not attested: the medieval parchment is lost and the text is known from Carlo Strozzi's transcription of about 1635, published only in the 2026 adhocnews article. The research pool tagged this attested; the verification pass downgraded it, and the downgrade is followed here. Notary, parish, witnesses, and property description were confirmed verbatim against the published transcription.
stops.campa: In the hand of the notary Giunta di Spigliato di Brunetto, of the people of Santa Lucia dei Magnoli, Simone sells the al Buco land and house on to Cecchino. Gualterotto and Ruggero, sons of the late Rosso, witness it, and Maffeo di Tommasino di Gualterotto de' Bardi with them. The property is the same al Buco land the two brothers bought together eight months before. The wife's consent is required for the transfer, so the wife is named. She is Bice, she is about fifteen, and she gives her consent before the witnesses.
stops.quote: l'unico atto esistente in cui compare in prima persona Beatrice Portinari
stops.quote_source: Domenico Savini and Samuele Masi, 'Messer Simone e madonna Bice: nuovi e inediti documenti su Beatrice Portinari', adhocnews.it, 17 July 2026
sources: Domenico Savini and Samuele Masi, adhocnews.it, 17 July 2026
BNCF, Magliabechiana cl. XXV n. 591 (olim Carte Strozziane 1223), Carlo Strozzi transcription, c.1635
Domenico Savini, presentation at Villa Bertelli, Forte dei Marmi, 1 March 2024
suggested_refs: The church of Santa Lucia dei Magnoli, Via de' Bardi, home parish of the notary Giunta di Spigliato

segments.name: Volterra, Prato, and the Widower's Year

stops.name: Volterra, the year as podesta
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year 1288 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which gives no month, day, or term length. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Volterra sits on its cliff above the Cecina valley, an old bishops' town that has been swallowing its own hillside for a thousand years. Like every Italian commune it hires its chief magistrate from outside, precisely so that he owes nothing to any faction inside the walls. For a term it hires Simone. This is the first office the record gives him, the ordinary opening of a Florentine magnate's public career. He judges, he keeps the peace, he holds the sword of a city not his own and then hands it back.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: The Palazzo dei Priori of Volterra, seat of the podesteria

stops.name: Florence, fifty lire in Folco Portinari's will
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and the single most secure document in the file. The testament is dated 15 January 1288 in D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice on Folco Portinari and in the Archivio di Stato di Firenze exhibition material; English and Italian Wikipedia date it 1287, a Florentine-style discrepancy recorded here and not resolved. The clause does not name Simone's father. Pin inherited from dante.journey.json.
stops.campa: Folco Portinari, dying, has ser Tedaldo Rustichelli draw his testament. He provides for the unmarried daughters at some eight hundred lire apiece, the sums that will buy them husbands. To Bice, already married and already dowered, he leaves fifty lire in small florins and one clause of Latin. That clause is the firmest thing anyone knows about Simone de' Bardi. It gives him no birth, no death, and no face. It gives a dying man in Florence calling a woman his daughter and this man's wife, on the fifteenth of January 1288.
stops.quote: Item domine Bici etiam filie sue, et uxori domini Simonis de Bardis, legavit de bonis suis libras l ad florenos
stops.quote_source: Folco Portinari's testament, 15 January 1288, printed by Isidoro Del Lungo, Beatrice nella vita e nella poesia del secolo XIII (Milan: Hoepli, 1891), documentary appendix; ASFi, Diplomatico, R. Acquisto Manni, 1288 gennaio 15, rogated by ser Tedaldo di Orlando Rustichelli
sources: Isidoro Del Lungo, Beatrice nella vita e nella poesia del secolo XIII (Milan: Hoepli, 1891)
Maria Paola Zanoboni, 'Portinari, Beatrice', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani, 2016)
Archivio di Stato di Firenze, 'Dante tra le carte: le donne della vita di Dante, Beatrice', ex Mostra 55
suggested_refs: The testament of Folco Portinari, 15 January 1288, ASFi Diplomatico
Paget Toynbee, Dante Alighieri: His Life and Works, quoting the same clause

stops.name: Prato, captain of the people
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year 1290 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice; no month, day, or term length is given. Month and day defaulted. No record connects the office to his wife's death in the same year, and nothing places him anywhere in particular that June.
stops.campa: Prato lies a morning's ride northwest, in the plain under the Calvana. Simone takes the captaincy of the people there, an office invented to hold the guilds and the popolani against exactly the sort of man he is: a magnate, a knight, kin to towers. He is holding it, or has just laid it down, in the year his wife dies. Communes hire such men anyway, from outside, because an outsider magnate has no cousins in the local vendetta. How long Simone's term ran, nobody wrote down. The office runs a fixed stretch, and then the outsider goes home.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Pretorio of Prato, Piazza del Comune

stops.name: Florence, the death of Bice
stops.date_confidence: The year 1290 is secure. The day is not: Zanoboni's Dizionario Biografico gives 19 June 1290, Marco Santagata calculates 8 June, and dante.journey.json carries 8 June. The discrepancy is calendrical and textual, the date being encoded numerologically rather than recorded documentarily, and it is not evidence of two deaths. Left open. The place of death is nowhere recorded; the Bardi houses are an inference from marital residence.
stops.campa: She dies at twenty-four. No document records the cause, the room, the hour, or where her husband was that day. What survives instead is arithmetic. Across the river Dante Alighieri, who never names Simone anywhere in his works and may never have spoken a word to him, encodes her death in the Vita Nova by counting the perfect number into itself, and scholars have been converting that sum into a calendar ever since, arriving at the eighth of June or the nineteenth. Simone's own documents run on for twenty-five more years. None of them mentions her.
stops.quote: era stata anima nobile di mona Biatrice figliuola cheffu [di messer] Folco de' Portinari di Firenze e moglie che fue di messer Simone di Geri de' Bardi di Firenze
stops.quote_source: Vernacular chiosa to Inferno II, MS Firenze, Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale II.I.39, printed by Luigi Rocca, 'Beatrice Portinari', Giornale dantesco XI (1903), p. 142
sources: Maria Paola Zanoboni, 'Portinari, Beatrice', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani, 2016)
Luigi Rocca, 'Beatrice Portinari', Giornale dantesco XI (1903)
Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: Dante, Vita Nova, the chapter encoding the date of Beatrice's death
The attribution dispute over the vernacular chiosa: Graziolo de' Bambaglioli's volgarizzatore, or Andrea Lancia's autograph of 1341-43

stops.name: Santa Margherita de' Cerchi, the tomb the city shows
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, not record. Zanoboni's Dizionario Biografico entry calls the modern marker unreliable, and Italian scholarship calls burial here 'assai improbabile', noting that Folco Portinari and Monna Tessa lie in the church but that a woman married into the Bardi would belong in the Bardi sepulchre. Dated to the month after the death only to order the segment; no burial date for Bice is recorded anywhere. Pin inherited from dante.journey.json.
stops.campa: A few steps from the Portinari houses stands a small church where Folco and his wife Monna Tessa lie, and where visitors are shown a marker and told that Bice lies there too. The scholarship does not support the claim. A woman married into the Bardi belonged at her death to the Bardi, and the earliest commentators who name her husband say nothing whatever about where she was put. Zanoboni calls the modern marker unreliable evidence. People go on leaving letters at it, asking for help with love.
stops.quote: ipsa domina erat anima generose domine Beatrice condam domini...
stops.quote_source: Graziolo de' Bambaglioli, Latin commentary on Inferno II (1324), quoted in Ernst Robert Curtius, European Literature and the Latin Middle Ages
sources: Maria Paola Zanoboni, 'Portinari, Beatrice', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani, 2016)
Ernst Robert Curtius, European Literature and the Latin Middle Ages, Dante chapter
suggested_refs: The church of Santa Margherita de' Cerchi, Via Santa Margherita, Florence, and its modern Beatrice marker
The commemorative plaque at Santa Maria Nuova, likewise flagged unreliable by Zanoboni

stops.name: Santa Croce, the Bardi sepulchre
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Three rival burial sites are on offer, Santa Margherita de' Cerchi, the Bardi ground at Santa Croce (Savini, 2008), and the Oltrarno parishes of Santa Lucia dei Magnoli or Santa Maria Sopr'Arno (Santagata), and no evidence decides between them. The contradiction is left open. Dated 1290 only to order the segment. Giotto's Bardi Chapel frescoes here postdate this stop by a generation and are family patronage, not Simone's. Pin inherited from al_kamil.journey.json and saint_francis.journey.json.
stops.campa: The other candidate is the Franciscan basilica, where the Bardi keep their chapels and their dead in the great cloister. Domenico Savini argued in 2008 for this ground. Marco Santagata argues instead for the Oltrarno parish churches, Santa Lucia dei Magnoli or Santa Maria Sopr'Arno, on the plain reasoning that people were buried where they lived. There are no bones, no inscription, and no notarial record of a funeral. Three sites are on offer and nothing decides between them.
sources: Maria Paola Zanoboni, 'Portinari, Beatrice', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani, 2016), citing Savini 2008
Marco Santagata's reconstruction, as summarized in the consulted secondary literature
suggested_refs: The Bardi sepulchre in the Great Cloister of Santa Croce, Florence
Giotto, The Trial by Fire before the Sultan, Bardi Chapel, Santa Croce, Florence, family patronage of a later generation

stops.name: Via de' Bardi, under the Ordinances of Justice
stops.date_confidence: The Ordinances of Justice are attested to 1293 as general Florentine history. Simone's own subjection to them is attested indirectly, through Del Lungo's notarial finding, reported by D'Addario, that he stood surety for Andrea de' Mozzi under the Ordinances. Dated 1293 to place the mechanism rather than an event in his life; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The popolo of Florence writes down what it has wanted for twenty years. The great families are named in a list, barred from the priorate, and made to post bond for their own conduct and their kinsmen's. The Bardi are on the list. Twice at least the bill will arrive at his own door. From here forward Simone's public life shows up in the record chiefly as an obligation: he stands behind other men's behaviour with his own money, and when they misbehave the commune comes to him for the money.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970), summarizing Isidoro Del Lungo
suggested_refs: The Ordinances of Justice of 1293 and the list of Florentine magnate houses

stops.name: San Piero Scheraggio, the peace of the Mannelli and Velluti
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 17 July 1295 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, summarizing Isidoro Del Lungo's documentary research. San Piero Scheraggio's surviving fabric now stands inside the Uffizi, and the coordinate is that site.
stops.campa: Two Oltrarno families have been killing each other, and the city makes them stop in public. This is what a magnate is for in a commune that distrusts magnates: his credit is the thing that makes another family's promise worth anything at all. In the old church of San Piero Scheraggio, before the magistrates, before magnates and popolani standing in the same room, the Mannelli and the Velluti swear peace. Men of standing put their names behind the oath as guarantors, and Simone is one of them.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970), summarizing Isidoro Del Lungo
suggested_refs: The remains of San Piero Scheraggio, now inside the Uffizi, Florence

stops.name: Florence, surety for Inghiramo of Biserno
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1295 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice: Simone 'fu mallevadore nello stesso anno per il condottiero Inghiramo de' conti di Biserno'. The research pool had flagged this unconfirmed; the verification pass located it in the source and upgraded it, and the upgrade is followed here. No month or day is given; the Palazzo del Podesta as the site is inference from communal practice, not documented.
stops.campa: The same year he stands behind a soldier. Inghiramo, of the counts of Biserno, is a condottiere in the commune's pay, and someone of standing must guarantee to Florence that he will do what he has contracted to do. Simone guarantees it. What the contract required, whether Inghiramo performed, and what the guarantee cost are all absent from the record. The whole episode survives as one line recovered from a communal register by a nineteenth-century scholar working through the Bardi papers.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
Isidoro Del Lungo, Beatrice nella vita e nella poesia del secolo XIII (Milan: Hoepli, 1891)
suggested_refs: The Palazzo del Podesta, now the Bargello, Florence

stops.name: Florence, the plot of 1300
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the most consequential claim in circulation about Simone. It rests entirely on Marco Santagata's prosopographical attribution to Simone di Geri; the underlying judicial roll was not located, and the claim is absent from D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which is the standard reference. A check of the Corso Donati literature does not name Simone either. Treated as unresolved. Dated 1300 with month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: May Day brings street fighting between the Cerchi and the Donati, and the losing side goes looking for help outside the walls. Guido di Battifolle is to bring armed men in against the government. The plan is discovered. Corso Donati is condemned to death in his absence and his houses ordered pulled down; the lesser conspirators are fined, and Santagata's reconstruction puts Simone among them. If that identification holds, he stands on the far side of the quarrel from Dante Alighieri, a prior of Florence that summer, whom the winning faction will drive out for good.
sources: Marco Santagata's biographical reconstruction of Dante, as summarized in the consulted secondary literature
Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970), which does not carry the claim
suggested_refs: The May Day violence of 1300 and the Black Guelf takeover of Florence in 1301

stops.name: Val di Greve, the castle of the Stinche
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1304 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which names the castle as a Cavalcanti possession in the Val di Greve. The research pool wrongly reported this absent from the source; the verification pass found it stated plainly. The coordinate is approximate, the ruin not being precisely sited in any accessible source; 43.545, 11.343 is the ridge between Panzano, Lamole and Radda. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: South of Greve, in the ridge country between Panzano and Radda, the Cavalcanti hold a castle called the Stinche. A Florentine force goes out to take it and Simone rides with them. The prisoners are marched back to the city and shut in a new pen the commune has been building near Santa Croce, and the pen keeps the castle's name for four hundred years afterward, so that le Stinche means a Florentine jail long after nobody can find the walls it was named for. The castle itself is gone.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: The Florentine prison of the Stinche, begun 1299 at the site of the present Teatro Verdi, named from the castle after 1304

stops.name: Palazzo dei Mozzi, the surety comes due
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Del Lungo's notarial research as reported by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which names messer Andrea di messer Tommaso de' Mozzi and the surety. The research pool wrongly reported this absent from the source. The year is inferred from the 22 May 1305 procuration that follows; month and day defaulted. The Palazzo dei Mozzi is the family's documented seat, not the recorded site of the transaction.
stops.campa: Andrea, son of messer Tommaso de' Mozzi, beats a popolano in the street. Under the Ordinances that is not a private quarrel; it is the offence the whole apparatus exists to punish, and it is the guarantor who pays. Simone had stood surety for him. Simone pays. The Mozzi then cede him assets in recompense. Their great house stands a few doors along the same bank of the river from his own, so the property that settles the beating of a popolano moves from one magnate family to another and never leaves the Oltrarno.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970), summarizing Isidoro Del Lungo
suggested_refs: The Palazzo dei Mozzi, Piazza dei Mozzi, Oltrarno, Florence

stops.name: Florence, the procuration to Cecchino
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 22 May 1305 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, citing Del Lungo. The research pool wrongly reported this absent from the source. The site of the act is not documented; the coordinate is the Palazzo del Podesta, by inference from communal practice.
stops.campa: It is the same partnership that bought al Buco a quarter of a century earlier and sold it back across a winter: one brother's name on the obligation, the other brother's feet on the ground. Whatever the two of them were to each other, the notaries did not write it down. They wrote down that neither is ever found acting alone. To collect what the Mozzi have ceded, Simone appoints his brother, and on the twenty-second of May Cecchino di Geri takes the procuration and rides out to take possession.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970), citing Isidoro Del Lungo
suggested_refs: The procuration of 22 May 1305 to Cecchino di Geri de' Bardi

stops.name: Val di Greve, buying Moriano from Vanni de' Mozzi
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 20 April 1306 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice. The coordinate is approximate: the source confirms the transaction and the date but does not site the castle precisely within the Val di Greve, and no accessible source establishes the ruin's exact position.
stops.campa: The recompense turns into a castle. On the twentieth of April Simone buys Moriano in the Val di Greve, with other holdings, from Vanni de' Mozzi. For a Florentine magnate a fortified place in the Chianti hills, with land under it and men on the land, is not a country retreat; it is a second base, stone and tenants at a day's ride from the city, held outside the reach of the priors. Moriano is the largest thing he ever acquires that the record troubles to name.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: The castle of Moriano, Val di Greve, Chianti

stops.name: Moriano, put out to rent
stops.date_confidence: Attested by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which records that he leased out the holdings some months after the April purchase. The research pool wrongly reported this absent from the source. The month is not given and is set to September only to place the lease after the purchase within the year.
stops.campa: Some months later he leases it out. Whatever Moriano is worth to him, it is not worth living in; he takes the rent and stays in the city. A man who spends his life standing surety needs a property he can pledge, so the castle becomes a line of income rather than a seat. This is the pattern of every property act the record gives him: land bought from kin, land sold to a brother, land taken in settlement of another man's crime, land let out to tenants.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: The lease of the Moriano estate, 1306

stops.name: Moriano, sold to the inquisitor
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 7 December 1307 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which names the purchaser only by office, as the inquisitor of heretical depravity. The characterization of inquisitorial finance in Tuscany is general background and is not stated in the source.
stops.campa: Twenty months after buying it he sells the castle to the inquisitor of heretical depravity. The office is Franciscan, it is funded out of the confiscated goods of the condemned, and in these years in Tuscany it is buying real property with the proceeds. Nothing in the record says what Simone thought of his purchaser, or whether he asked where the money came from. After this sale the Chianti disappears from his file. The deed is dated the seventh of December 1307.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: The office of the inquisitor of heretical depravity in Tuscany and its property dealings

stops.name: Arezzo, the first campaign
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1308 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which gives the year and no further detail. Month and day defaulted. The coordinate is the historic centre of Arezzo; the source does not specify where the operations took place.
stops.campa: Florence goes out against Arezzo again, as it has been doing on and off since Campaldino nineteen years earlier, and Simone rides out with the host. He is past forty and possibly past fifty. This is the shape of most of what is known about him: he is present at things, and the record does not say what he was like when he was present. Of Arezzo in 1308 nothing survives but his name in a list of the men who went. No wound, no ransom, no captured banner.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: The Florentine campaigns against Arezzo, 1308 and 1310

stops.name: Orvieto, captain of the people
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1310 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which records the Orvieto captaincy and operations against Arezzo in the same year without reconciling them. That tension is recorded and not resolved. Month, day, and term length are not given and are defaulted.
stops.campa: Orvieto stands on its tufa cliff south of the Tuscan border, a papal town, Guelf, with its own factions eating it from the inside. It hires Simone as captain of the people. He is a long way from the Arno now, a Florentine knight administering a stranger city's popolo, and it is the third such magistracy the record gives him after Volterra and Prato. In the same year, on the same authority, he is also in arms against Arezzo. How one man does both is not explained.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: The Palazzo del Popolo, Orvieto

stops.name: Arezzo, the second campaign
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1310 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice. The relation between this campaign and the Orvieto captaincy of the same year is not specified in the source and is not invented here. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The name appears in the Aretine operations a second time. Between 1308 and 1315 Simone is a man who turns out when Florence musters, which by this date is often: the city is fighting Arezzo, watching Pisa, and preparing for an emperor. What the operations of that year achieved, and whether he was out for a week or a season, the notice does not report. There is no indication he commanded anything, or that anybody expected him to. He is one of the mounted men the commune can call, and the calling is recorded because the commune wrote down who came.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
suggested_refs: Florentine communal muster rolls of the early fourteenth century

stops.name: Florence, against Henry VII
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1313 by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which counts Simone among the Florentines firmly opposed to Henry VII. The site is inference: the Palazzo della Signoria is where such civic resolutions were taken, but no document places Simone there. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Henry of Luxembourg comes down into Italy to be crowned and to make the empire real again, and Florence refuses him with the whole weight of its Guelf conviction. Simone is counted among the firm ones. The two men take opposite sides of the same question, one inside the walls and one shut out of them, and neither ever mentions the other in a surviving line. In those same years Dante Alighieri, in exile, is writing letters to that emperor urging him on, calling the city that threw him out a viper turning on its own vitals.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
Marco Santagata's biographical reconstruction of Dante, as summarized in the consulted secondary literature
suggested_refs: Dante's epistles to Henry VII and to the princes and peoples of Italy, 1310-1311

stops.name: Via de' Bardi, the marriage of Francesca
stops.date_confidence: Reported. The 1313 document was presented publicly by Domenico Savini at Villa Bertelli, Forte dei Marmi, on 1 March 2024 and is not in D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice; the research pool's citation to D'Addario was wrong and is corrected here. Savini calls Francesca Simone's daughter. The Strozzi groom is variously named Francesco di Pierozzo, Pinaccio, or Pierozzo in modern accounts and no source settles it. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: A daughter is married to a Strozzi. Her name is Francesca, and the act does not name her mother. Simone's known children are Bartola, born of Gemma dei Pulci, Gemma, who marries an Ardingo de' Medici, and this Francesca. Francesca's mother is not named in any document that survives, and of the ten years he was married to Bice Portinari the Dizionario Biografico says flatly that no children are shown to have come. The Strozzi groom is called Francesco di Pierozzo in one modern account, Pinaccio in another, and Pierozzo in a third.
sources: Domenico Savini, presentation at Villa Bertelli, Forte dei Marmi, 1 March 2024
Maria Paola Zanoboni, 'Portinari, Beatrice', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani, 2016)
suggested_refs: The 1313 marriage act of Francesca di Simone de' Bardi to a Strozzi, presented by Savini in 2024 and not yet critically published

stops.name: Montecatini, the plain under the town
stops.date_confidence: Attested by D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice; the battle date of 29 August 1315 is independently corroborated. The coordinate is the plain at Montecatini Terme, where the battle was fought, not the hill town of Montecatini Alto at 43.8964, 10.7894; the research pool labelled the pin Montecatini Alto while giving the plain's coordinate, and the label is corrected here. Simone's personal outcome is recorded nowhere.
stops.campa: Uguccione della Faggiola brings Pisa and Lucca down on the Guelf army on the flat ground below Montecatini, and the day goes very badly. Thousands of Florentines and their allies are killed and the rest are driven back through the marsh ditches. Simone is reported in arms there. Whether he was killed, taken, wounded, or rode off unharmed is not recorded, and the documents that can safely be called his end here. The Guelf dead are still being counted days afterward, and the count keeps rising.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
Wikipedia, 'Battle of Montecatini', for date and location
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Montecatini, 29 August 1315, on the plain of the Val di Nievole

stops.name: Florence, the codicil with no shelfmark
stops.date_confidence: Reported and unverified. The proposed 7 September 1321 codicil is known only from Savini and Masi's 2026 popular article; the full text, notary, hospital, archive, and shelfmark were not published and could not be located. It contradicts the 1329 San Miniato record below, and the contradiction is left open. Treated as an announced claim awaiting archival publication, not an established document.
stops.campa: A 2026 article promises the last will of messer Simone di Geri de' Bardi: dictated in a Florentine hospital under his own family's patronage on the seventh of September, dead within days, a week before Dante Alighieri dies at Ravenna. It is a very satisfying ending. The article's own table of contents names the codicil; its text supplies no notary, no hospital, no archive, and no shelfmark, and no critical edition has printed it. So far it is an announcement.
sources: Domenico Savini and Samuele Masi, 'Messer Simone e madonna Bice: nuovi e inediti documenti su Beatrice Portinari', adhocnews.it, 17 July 2026
suggested_refs: The announced codicil and last will of messer Simone di Geri de' Bardi, unpublished

stops.name: San Miniato, dominus Symon de Bardis
stops.date_confidence: The record is attested (ASFi, Provvisioni 25, fol. 88v, cited by Del Lungo and reported by D'Addario), but the identification with Beatrice's husband is treated as conditional by D'Addario himself, owing to Bardi homonymy. It stands in direct contradiction with the proposed death of 1321, and that contradiction is left open. Del Lungo himself believed the documented life ended after 1315.
stops.campa: In the Florentine Provvisioni for December 1329 a dominus Symon de Bardis is given the captaincy of the people of San Miniato, six months to run from the tenth of February following. If it is him, he is nearly seventy and still riding out to govern other people's towns, and the deathbed of 1321 never happened. The Bardi also produced Simone di Nello, Simone di Giuliano, Simone del fu Cino, and Simone di messer Iacopo. Which one did the clerk mean? D'Addario will not say.
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970), citing Isidoro Del Lungo and ASFi, Provvisioni 25, fol. 88v
suggested_refs: ASFi, Provvisioni 25, fol. 88v, the appointment of 18 December 1329

stops.name: Santa Croce, no grave
stops.date_confidence: No death date, burial place, or tomb is recorded for Simone anywhere. The negative finding is confirmed in D'Addario's Enciclopedia Dantesca notice, which carries none, and in the University of Virginia and IATH Florentine Sepoltuario database, whose entry for Simone messer di M. Geri di Ricco di Bardo carries genealogy and a manuscript reference and no burial data. Dated 1330 only to close the file after the last record that may be his. Pin inherited from al_kamil.journey.json and saint_francis.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Bardi bury their dead in the great cloister of Santa Croce. No stone there names Simone. The registers of Florentine tombs carry his genealogy and a manuscript reference and no burial at all. He wrote nothing: no letter, no speech, no line of verse survives in his hand or his voice, and every word attached to him was set down by a notary describing what he did with property. Boccaccio, eighty years after the marriage, gives him the only description anybody has. It is seven words long and it is not about him.
stops.quote: e fu moglie d'un cavaliere de' Bardi, chiamato messer Simone
stops.quote_source: Giovanni Boccaccio, Esposizioni sopra la Comedia di Dante, literal exposition of Inferno II, 1373-74
sources: Arnaldo D'Addario, 'Bardi, Simone', Enciclopedia Dantesca (Treccani, 1970)
University of Virginia and IATH, Florentine Sepoltuario, entry 152, 'Simone (messer) di M. Geri di Ricco di Bardo'
Giovanni Boccaccio, Esposizioni sopra la Comedia di Dante (1373-74)
suggested_refs: The Great Cloister of Santa Croce and the Bardi burials
Isidoro Del Lungo, Beatrice nella vita e nella poesia del secolo XIII (Milan: Hoepli, 1891), the study that separated this Simone from his namesakes
